title: Why God became man (ST III.1)
hook: Thomas speaks of fittingness: nothing more fitting than God sharing our nature

segments.voice: Yesterday, grace: God's help, which heals our nature and lifts it, and doesn't destroy it. Your line was help is needed. Before which task did you ask? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-seven.

Her friend's father has died, across the country. A card would be kind. Flowers would be kind. A long phone call would be more than kind. Nobody expects anything else. Instead she books a flight, takes time off work, and is standing on the porch when the door opens. She didn't have to. Nothing required it. But everyone in that house knows it was exactly the right thing, the thing that fit. Thomas Aquinas opens the third part of his Summa with that kind of question about God. Could God have helped us another way? And if so, why become one of us?
screen: `A CARD WOULD HAVE BEEN KIND.` → `SHE SHOWS UP AT THE DOOR.` → `WHY BECOME ONE OF US?`

segments.voice: Thomas's key word here is fitting. Not necessary. Fitting. He starts with what God is. God is goodness itself. And goodness, Thomas says, following an old Christian writer named Dionysius, is the kind of thing that pours itself out. It shares. So it belongs to the highest good to share itself in the highest way. And what higher way could there be than joining a created nature to himself, so that God and a human being are one person? That's the incarnation: John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." Then Thomas asks the sharper question. Was it necessary? Couldn't God simply have forgiven, by a word? Thomas says yes, God could have. Nothing forced his hand. But some things are needed the way a horse is needed for a journey: not because the journey is impossible without it, but because it goes so much better. And then he lists what this way does. It gives faith firmer footing, because God himself is the one speaking. It gives hope. It stirs love, because nothing moves a person to love like being loved first. It gives an example to follow. And it opens the door to a surprising gift: sharing in God's own life. Thomas quotes Augustine's bold line: God became man so that man might become God. Second Peter says it in its own words: "partakers of the divine nature." So Thomas's answer to why is not a mechanism. It's a kind of beauty. Of all the ways God might have helped, Thomas sees none that fits better than coming in person and standing at the door.
screen: `FITTING, NOT NECESSARY.` · `GOODNESS POURS ITSELF OUT.` · `A HORSE FOR A JOURNEY.` · `FAITH, HOPE, LOVE, EXAMPLE, SHARING.` · then, large: `THE WORD WAS MADE FLESH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wonder at the incarnation. Settle, and breathe. Look at your own hands for a moment. Ordinary hands: knuckles, lines, maybe a scar. Christians say God had hands like these, that got tired, and cut, and held people. Let that sit, without trying to solve it. If you pray, you can slowly say the line from John, "the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us," and rest on one word of it. If you don't pray, simply notice what it would mean to someone to believe that. The bell holds the time.
Why God became man. Thomas's answer: not because God had to, but because, for the highest good, sharing itself in person was the most fitting way. Today's word.
Your line: most fitting. Today, find one place where a text would do, and show up in person instead, or make the call. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Catholics profess the incarnation in the Creed at Sunday Mass, bowing at the words about Christ becoming man, and kneeling at those words on Christmas and the Annunciation.

fork.reveal: Thomas says God could have done it otherwise. the incarnation was needed like a horse for a journey: not required, but far better.

original.note: Latin, the language Thomas wrote in: fittingness, the way things come together well.

trapdoor: what you thought: God became man because he had no choice.
what it means: for Thomas, it wasn't necessary but fitting: the highest good sharing itself in the highest way.
what a scholar hears: Thomas's argument from convenientia, fittingness, with Dionysius's maxim that the good pours itself out.

sources.quoted: And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us

notes: All Aquinas is paraphrased. Check: God's nature is goodness; the good is self-communicative (Dionysius, Divine Names 4); it belongs to the highest good to communicate itself in the highest manner, which is the union of created nature to God in one person (III.1.1); necessity of the end, 'as a horse is necessary for a journey', and God could have restored humanity otherwise (III.1.2); the list of benefits (faith, hope, charity, example, participation in the divinity), and Augustine's 'God was made man, that man might be made God' quoted in III.1.2.
Dionysius is called 'an old Christian writer' with no date or identity claims; confirm.
howItsDone: bowing at 'and by the Holy Spirit was incarnate' in the Creed, and genuflecting on Christmas and the Annunciation (GIRM 137); confirm.
Douay-Rheims wording to confirm: John 1:14 and 2 Peter 1:4 (fragments).
